title: Code Review & Collaboration
summary: The cheapest place to catch a bug, the fastest way to spread knowledge — but only if the diffs stay small and the feedback stays kind.

blocks.markdown:
Code review is a second pair of eyes on a change before it ships.

- The author opens a **pull request (PR)** — a proposed diff; a reviewer reads it, comments, and approves so it can **merge**.
- It's not just bug-catching: it **spreads knowledge**, enforces **shared standards**, and records *why* a change was made.
- A quality gate **and** a conversation between peers.
- The most reliable, cheapest quality lever a team has.

blocks.subTitle: Why it exists
blocks.markdown:
Review was forced into existence once teams grew past one person.

- **Bugs get ~10x cheaper** to fix at each earlier stage they're caught — review is the last cheap stage before production.
- **Knowledge spreads.** Reviewing Alice's billing PRs slowly teaches Bob billing too, raising the **bus factor**.
- **Consistency holds.** Left alone a codebase drifts into ten ways to do one thing; review applies standards change by change.
- A quiet fourth win: an **audit trail** of decisions.

blocks.subTitle: The review loop
blocks.markdown:
The mechanics are a small state machine.

![Code review flow from open PR to merge](assets/d09-code-review-collaboration/review-flow.svg)

- Author opens a PR with a clear title and *why*; **automated checks** run (tests, lint, build, scans).
- Reviewer leaves comments anchored to lines: **blocking**, **suggestion**, or **nit**.
- Author replies, pushes fixes, re-requests review — the **re-review** back-arrow is the part people forget.
- One (or N) approvals + green checks → it merges, then ships.

assets.alt: Code review flow from open PR to merge

blocks.subTitle: What to look for, in order
blocks.markdown:
Reviewer attention is finite — spend it top-down.

![Grouped checklist of what to review](assets/d09-code-review-collaboration/review-checklist.svg)

- **Correctness** — edge cases, nulls, races, error paths. Where real bugs hide.
- **Design** — right shape, right layer; highest-leverage and hardest to fix later.
- **Tests**, then **readability**, then **security** and **performance** where they matter.
- **Style last** — if a machine can check it, a machine should ([d04-testing-quality](d04-testing-quality.md), [c08-cryptography-security](c08-cryptography-security.md)).

assets.alt: Grouped checklist of what to review

blocks.subTitle: Small PRs are the whole game
blocks.markdown:
Small PRs aren't a nicety — they're the only way review actually works.

- Effectiveness drops sharply past **~400 lines** in one sitting; defect-finding falls off a cliff.
- Review **no faster than ~300–500 LOC/hour** and keep sessions **under ~60 min** — attention degrades.
- A 50-line PR gets read line by line; a 1,500-line PR gets a 90-second skim and a "LGTM."
- That skim is **review theater**, not review.

blocks.subTitle: Giving feedback
blocks.markdown:
Feedback should be kind, specific, and actionable.

- Say **what's wrong, why it matters, and how to fix it** — and critique the code, never the person.
- Ask questions over orders: "what happens if this is null?" beats "this is broken."
- Tag **severity**: a blocking issue must be fixed; a trivial one gets a `nit:` prefix the author can ignore.
- Praise the good parts too — review isn't only negative.

blocks.subTitle: The core tensions
blocks.markdown:
Good review matches depth to risk rather than maxing one dial.

| Tension | Resolve by |
|---|---|
| Thorough vs fast | Match depth to risk |
| Perfect vs shipping | Approve if it's an improvement |
| Author taste vs yours | Author wins if correct |
| Async thread vs call | Talk after two round-trips |

Google's written rule: approve once the change **improves overall code health**, even if imperfect.

blocks.subTitle: Decision rules
blocks.markdown:
Plain-English rules for the common situations.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Touches auth, money, data | Block until correct |
| Pure formatting | Let the linter, not you |
| Refactor + feature mixed | Ask to split first |
| Correct, not your style | Approve, maybe a nit |
| Deadlocked on taste | Escalate to a tech lead |

blocks.subTitle: How big shops do it
blocks.markdown:
Across the industry the pattern is: automate the mechanical, reserve humans for judgment.

- **Google** — review is mandatory; the standard is "improves code health," and linters handle the commas.
- **Linux kernel** — a **maintainer hierarchy** scales review to thousands; its harsh tone is a cautionary tale.
- **GitHub/GitLab** — branch protection encodes the gate: no merge to `main` without N approvals + green CI ([d05-git-version-control](d05-git-version-control.md)).
- **Amazon/Meta** — bots catch null checks and anti-patterns so humans focus on design.

blocks.subTitle: A money-touching PR
blocks.markdown:
Walk one real diff and the bugs surface fast.

```sql
SELECT pct FROM codes WHERE code = '" + code + "'
```

- **Security (hard block):** `code` concatenated into SQL → injection. Use a parameterized query.
- **Correctness:** a missing code → `discount` is null → the math breaks. Handle it.
- **Bad data:** clamp discount to 0–100 so a stray row can't make totals negative.
- **Tests:** money logic with zero tests is a real gap — cover valid, missing, out-of-range, empty.

blocks.subTitle: Signals it's healthy
blocks.markdown:
No dashboards — these are the signals a Staff engineer watches.

- **Time-to-first-review** in hours, not days — slow review kills momentum.
- **PR size** mostly under ~200–400 lines; a fat tail of 1,000+ liners is being rubber-stamped.
- **One to three review rounds** — zero means rubber-stamping, many means bikeshedding or half-baked PRs.
- **Comment quality over count**, balanced reviewer load, and authors who don't dread opening PRs.

The failure modes that drain the value out of review:

- **Nitpicking** — drowning a PR in trivia instead of focusing on what matters.
- **Bikeshedding** — arguing the trivial (a button color) because it's easy, while the hard stuff slides.
- **Rubber-stamping** — approving without reading; worse than no review, it breeds false confidence.
- **Blocking on taste** — vetoing correct code because it's not how you'd write it.
- **More reviewers ≠ better** — past two you get diffusion of responsibility and nobody checks deeply.
